name: Haitian Creole
variety: Standard Haitian Creole based on the speech of Port-au-Prince and the west, in the official spelling of 1979-1980
sources: Valdman, Albert (2015). Haitian Creole: Structure, Variation, Status, Origin. Sheffield: Equinox.
Valdman, Albert (1978). Le créole: structure, statut et origine. Paris: Klincksieck.
Tinelli, Henri (1981). Creole Phonology. The Hague: Mouton.
Dejean, Yves (1980). Comment écrire le créole d'Haïti. Outremont: Collectif Paroles.
Cadely, Jean-Robert (2002). Le statut des voyelles nasales en créole haïtien. Lingua 112.
Fattier, Dominique (2013). Haitian Creole. In Michaelis, Maurer, Haspelmath and Huber (eds.), The Survey of Pidgin and Creole Languages, volume II. Oxford University Press.
contrasts: seven oral vowels /i e ɛ a ɔ o u/, with close-mid versus open-mid marked in the spelling (e versus è, o versus ò): pe 'be quiet' versus pè 'priest, fear'; bo 'kiss' versus bò 'side'

three nasal vowels /ɛ̃ ã ɔ̃/ (written en, an, on) against the oral vowels and against oral vowel plus nasal consonant: pan [pã] 'peacock' versus pàn [pan] 'breakdown'; pen [pɛ̃] 'bread' versus pèn [pɛn] 'pain'; bon [bɔ̃] versus bòn [bɔn] 'maid'
nasal vowel plus nasal consonant is a further possibility (written ann, enn, onn, anm): pann [pãn] 'to hang', venn [vɛ̃n] 'vein', chanm [ʃãm] 'room'
voiced versus voiceless stops and fricatives, including /ʃ ʒ/ (ch, j)
/ɣ/ (written r) versus /w/, only before unrounded vowels
no front rounded vowels in the basic variety: French u, eu correspond to /i/, /e/ or /ɛ/ (diri 'rice', ble 'blue')
high nasal vowels [ĩ ũ] are marginal (a few words of African origin and Vodou terms, as in oungan)
allophony: /ɣ/ is a weak velar fricative or approximant, never a trill; it does not occur before rounded vowels, where /w/ is found instead (wouj 'red', wòch 'stone'), nor at the end of a syllable (pòt 'door', fè 'to do')

oral vowels are nasalised next to nasal consonants, in varying degree: regressive nasalisation before a nasal consonant and progressive nasalisation after one (mwen [mwɛ̃], nen [nɛ̃]); much of this is fixed in the spelling (fanmi, lanmè)
the postposed determiner la changes with the end of the preceding word: la, a, an, nan, lan
/ɥ/ occurs only before /i/ (uit 'eight', lannuit) and many speakers replace it with /w/
/h/ is marginal and regional; most speakers of the standard have no /h/
/tʃ dʒ/ are rare and found in expressive words, loanwords and words with older ti, di, gu before a vowel (tchatcha, djòl, djab)
French-influenced speech (kreyòl swa) adds front rounded vowels [y ø œ] and post-vocalic r
unstressed short forms of pronouns lose their vowel in running speech (mwen as m, li as l, ou as w)
syllable_structure: (C)(C)V(C); final clusters of French are simplified (tab, kat, pòs)
phonotactics: onset clusters are obstruent plus l, ɣ or a glide (pran, bwa, dlo, gwo, twa)
no /ɣ/ in the coda; words end in a vowel, a single consonant or, rarely, a cluster with s
nasal vowels do not contrast with oral ones before nasal consonants in many words, since regressive nasalisation applies

stress.rule: Prominence falls on the last syllable of the word, and in connected speech on the last syllable of the rhythmic group; postposed determiners and pronouns form part of the group.
stress.cues: duration (lengthening of the final syllable) and pitch movement; intensity plays little part

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in quality; short forms of function words lose their vowel
rhythm.notes: No rhythm measurements for Haitian Creole are cited here; the classification follows the descriptive literature and the French-like phrase-final prominence.

length.notes: No length contrast. Nasal vowels are somewhat longer than oral ones, as in French; no figure is cited here.

intonation.declarative: rises at the end of non-final rhythmic groups and a fall to low on the last syllable of the utterance
intonation.yes_no_question: either the particle èske at the start with a statement-like contour, or no particle and a rise on the last syllable
intonation.wh_question: question word (ki, kisa, kote, kouman) first and high, then a fall to the end
intonation.continuation: rise on the last syllable of each non-final group
intonation.accent_shape: pitch movement on the last syllable of the group, rising when non-final and falling when final
intonation.notes: The intonation of Haitian Creole is little studied; the entries summarise the general statements of the grammars and should be read as low confidence.

problems: there are no nasal vowels in the output: an, en, on are read as oral vowel plus [n] (pan [pˈan], pen [pˈen], pon [pˈon], mwen [mwˈen], manje [manjˈe]); the phoneme table defines three nasal vowels but no rule uses them
è and ò are read as close [e] and [o] (bèl [bˈel], fò [fˈo], tèt [tˈet]), so the contrasts e versus è and o versus ò are lost; the open-mid phonemes of the table are unused
ou is read as three segments [o u u] (bonjou [bonjouˈu], nou [nouˈu], moun [mouˈun]) instead of [u]
j is read as the glide [j] instead of [ʒ] (jou, manje, bonjou)
r is read as [h] instead of the velar fricative [ɣ] (rat [hˈat], kreyòl [khejˈol], frè [fhˈe])
ch is read as [ʃ] followed by [h] (chante [ʃhantˈe], chèz [ʃhˈez], machin [maʃhˈin])
ui is two vowels [u i] instead of [ɥi] (uit), and final ng is [ŋɡ] instead of [ŋ] (bilding)

the number words in the word list are entered in ordinary spelling where phoneme codes are expected, so numbers are misread (1 is [yoˈun] with the French vowel [y], 5 is [sˈenk], 18 is [dizuˈit]), and 80 and 100 are given as French words with the French uvular r
only five pronouns are marked unstressed; there is no treatment of the short pronoun forms or of the determiner variants
no tune set is selected, so the generic default tunes are used
good: prominence is on the final syllable, as in the language
the plain consonants and the glides y [j], w are read correctly, and dj is [dʒ]

notes: The voice is marked as testing and has no maintainer. The rule file has about 100 lines with one rule per letter; it does not implement the digraphs of the official spelling (an, en, on, ou, ch, ui, oun, in, the grave accent). In practice the voice does not produce recognisable Haitian Creole, and the gap is in the rules rather than in the phoneme table.
